titleStmt.title: Graph schema validation at last? Revisiting the Stemmarest data model with Neo4J and SHACL
titleStmt.author: Tara Lee Andrews

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Graph schema validation at last? Revisiting the Stemmarest data model with Neo4J and SHACL

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: The variant graph data model used to represent text collations, and whether its constraints can be expressed formally.
span.quote: In 2020 there was an attempt to create an ontology (Andrews, 2020) for the variant graph, which is a data model used in tools such as CollateX (Haentjens Dekker et al., 2015), Stemmarest (Andrews, 2019), and TraVIZ (Jänicke et al., 2015) to represent and visualize text collations and certain sorts of annotation.

span.label: method
span.quote: This language solves exactly the problem that ontologies do not; specifically, in conjunction with a database that supports transactions and their rollbacks such as Neo4J, a set of SHACL constraints can ensure the consistency of data added to the graph, so that (to take the example above) a witness from one text tradition cannot be included in a stemma belonging to an entirely different tradition.

span.label: graph schema validation
span.quote: In this sense, the critics of graph-based models do have a point; how do we validate our graphs?

span.label: review
span.quote: Recently, however, there have been two intriguing developments in the Semantic Web world that are especially relevant to digital humanities projects, not least Stemmarest.

span.label: An ontology describes what kinds of thing exist and how they relate, but cannot forbid a combination that is well-typed and still wrong
span.quote: Thus, while the Stemmarest ontology can describe the data reasonably well, it is not an adequate tool for setting constraints; these must still be described in code.

span.label: The hard constraints are cross-object: an entity appearing in one structure must be consistent with its membership elsewhere
span.quote: For example, if a witness W appears in a stemma belonging to tradition A, the model software should ensure that W also belongs to tradition A as a witness and not, for example, an unrelated tradition B; moreover, W should not appear in any stemmata of tradition B.

span.label: Some constraints are global properties of the whole graph and cannot be checked object by object at all
span.quote: Even more intractable problems arise with more complex specifications: for example, the need to ensure that the variant graph is self-consistent, so that a user cannot create a situation in the model where a portion of the edited text loops back onto itself or is omitted altogether.

span.label: The original failure was not a modelling mistake but a mismatch of purpose - OWL was built for open-world inference and editors want description and consistency
span.quote: We would argue here that most editors are less interested in the sort of open-world inference for which OWL was intended (though Vogeler makes a case for why it might be interesting), as opposed to the formalisation, description, and consistency of their data.

span.label: Constraints only bite if the store can undo a rejected write, so validation needs transactions and rollback underneath it
span.quote: This language solves exactly the problem that ontologies do not; specifically, in conjunction with a database that supports transactions and their rollbacks such as Neo4J, a set of SHACL constraints can ensure the consistency of data added to the graph, so that (to take the example above) a witness from one text tradition cannot be included in a stemma belonging to an entirely different tradition.

span.label: Allowing arbitrary code inside constraints erases the code/data boundary that sustainability practice depends on, which the author treats as a feature
span.quote: In a sense, this affordance challenges the idea of the separation of program code and data that is the usual gold standard for sustainability efforts, insofar as constraints can be expressed as arbitrarily complex programming logic, embedded in RDF or Turtle files and saved as a schema alongside the data itself.

span.label: The author's own earlier Stemmarest ontology describes the data adequately but cannot express the model's constraints, which still have to be written in program code.
span.note: what this limits: any use of the ontology to enforce the model: WHILE THE STEMMAREST ONTOLOGY CAN DESCRIBE THE DATA REASONABLY WELL, IT IS NOT AN ADEQUATE TOOL FOR SETTING CONSTRAINTS; THESE MUST STILL BE DESCRIBED IN CODE
span.quote: Thus, while the Stemmarest ontology can describe the data reasonably well, it is not an adequate tool for setting constraints; these must still be described in code.

span.label: RDF*, the extension the interoperability half of the proposal depends on, is acknowledged to be immature.
span.note: what this limits: the interoperability half of the proposal: RDF* IS STILL IN AN EARLY PHASE OF DEVELOPMENT
span.quote: While it is still in an early phase of development, RDF* provides the long-awaited ability to set context for LOD statements, and promises to triple stores the same ability to set properties on relationships that graph databases such as Neo4J have always provided; this in turn has opened the way for Stemmarest, and many other projects besides, to take advantage of Neo4J’s powerful graph traversal and analysis algorithms while preserving full interoperability with LOD formats.

span.label: SHACL's SPARQL/Javascript constraint components undermine the separation of code from data that sustainability practice normally treats as the gold standard.
span.note: what this limits: the sustainability claim for SHACL: constraint components CHALLENGE THE IDEA OF THE SEPARATION OF PROGRAM CODE AND DATA THAT IS THE USUAL GOLD STANDARD
span.quote: In a sense, this affordance challenges the idea of the separation of program code and data that is the usual gold standard for sustainability efforts, insofar as constraints can be expressed as arbitrarily complex programming logic, embedded in RDF or Turtle files and saved as a schema alongside the data itself.

span.label: The 2020 ontology attempt failed because RDF and OWL handle property attributes badly, and the model depends on them
span.note: what this limits: any RDF/OWL serialisation of a property-bearing graph: THE ONTOLOGY WAS NOT SUITABLE FOR EXPRESSING THE FULL DATA MODEL ... NOT LEAST BECAUSE ALL OF THEM ... RELY ON PROP[erty attributes]
span.quote: The conclusion was that the ontology was not suitable for expressing the full data model employed in variant graphs, not least because all of them (Stemmarest most heavily) rely on property attributes, which RDF and OWL do not handle well and which can therefore not be suitably represented in an ontology definition.

span.label: The graph database's own constraint mechanism reaches only data properties, not structure
span.note: what this limits: the graph-database alternative: CONSTRAINT ENFORCEMENT IN NEO4J ... IS INDEED LIMITED STRICTLY TO DATA PROPERTIES OF NODES AND RELATIONSHIPS, not structure
span.quote: Constraint enforcement in Neo4J, perhaps the most popular graph database, is indeed limited strictly to data properties of nodes and relationships (Neo4J, Inc., 2022).

span.label: The extension that would fix the property problem is not yet mature
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 1 - the fix for the property problem is immature
span.quote: While it is still in an early phase of development, RDF* provides the long-awaited ability to set context for LOD statements, and promises to triple stores the same ability to set properties on relationships that graph databases such as Neo4J have always provided; this in turn has opened the way for Stemmarest, and many other projects besides, to take advantage of Neo4J’s powerful graph traversal and analysis algorithms while preserving full interoperability with LOD formats.

span.label: Linked-data stores are in no better position, having relied on ontologies alone
span.note: what this limits: the linked-data alternative: LOD STORES ... HAVE SO FAR DEPENDED MORE OR LESS ENTIRELY ON ONTOLOGY SPECIFICATIONS, WITH LIMITATIONS AS DESCRIBED ABOVE
span.quote: The situation is hardly better for LOD stores, which have so far depended more or less entirely on ontology specifications, with limitations as described above, to describe their data.

span.label: schema - as DESCRIPTION: says what classes exist and how they may relate, which an ontology does well
span.quote: While many of the classes used by Stemmarest and their relationships to each other can be described adequately in OWL, the model relies upon many additional constraints that, while seemingly simple, go beyond OWL’s capabilities.

span.label: schema - as CONSTRAINT: forbids configurations that are well-typed and still wrong, which is what validation actually needs
span.quote: However, one of the important aspects of validation is to prevent inattentive mistakes in the data model.

span.label: the graph problem - LOCAL: a property on a single node or relationship, which Neo4J can already enforce
span.quote: Constraint enforcement in Neo4J, perhaps the most popular graph database, is indeed limited strictly to data properties of nodes and relationships (Neo4J, Inc., 2022).

span.label: the graph problem - GLOBAL: a property of the whole graph, such as the edited text not looping back on itself, which nothing local can check
span.quote: Even more intractable problems arise with more complex specifications: for example, the need to ensure that the variant graph is self-consistent, so that a user cannot create a situation in the model where a portion of the edited text loops back onto itself or is omitted altogether.

span.label: OWL's purpose - as intended: open-world inference, deriving new facts from stated ones
span.quote: Vogeler (2021, p. 80) notes in his discussion of graph-based models for critical edition that “the formal affordance of OWL is not really exploited in Digital Scholarly Editions”.

span.label: OWL's purpose - as wanted by editors: formalisation, description and consistency, which is a different job it was not built for
span.quote: We would argue here that most editors are less interested in the sort of open-world inference for which OWL was intended (though Vogeler makes a case for why it might be interesting), as opposed to the formalisation, description, and consistency of their data.

span.label: claim_type: method
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: method — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: The second major development is SHACL (Shapes Constraint Language), a language whose purpose is to define a set of constraints against which RDF graphs can be validated (Knublauch and Kontokostas, 2017).

span.label: builds-on → Andrews (2020), the 2020 attempt to build an ontology for the variant graph / Stemmarest
span.quote: What the 2020 project showed, in the end, was the inadequacy of ontologies and especially OWL as a validation model for graph-based data.

span.label: extends → Vogeler (2021) on graph-based models for critical edition and the unexploited affordance of OWL
span.quote: We would argue here that most editors are less interested in the sort of open-world inference for which OWL was intended (though Vogeler makes a case for why it might be interesting), as opposed to the formalisation, description, and consistency of their data.

span.label: builds-on → SHACL (Shapes Constraint Language), Knublauch and Kontokostas (2017)
span.quote: This language solves exactly the problem that ontologies do not; specifically, in conjunction with a database that supports transactions and their rollbacks such as Neo4J, a set of SHACL constraints can ensure the consistency of data added to the graph, so that (to take the example above) a witness from one text tradition cannot be included in a stemma belonging to an entirely different tradition.

span.label: builds-on → RDF* (Arndt et al., 2021)
span.quote: While it is still in an early phase of development, RDF* provides the long-awaited ability to set context for LOD statements, and promises to triple stores the same ability to set properties on relationships that graph databases such as Neo4J have always provided; this in turn has opened the way for Stemmarest, and many other projects besides, to take advantage of Neo4J’s powerful graph traversal and analysis algorithms while preserving full interoperability with LOD formats.

span.label: critiques → the author's own 2020 attempt to build a variant-graph ontology
span.quote: What the 2020 project showed, in the end, was the inadequacy of ontologies and especially OWL as a validation model for graph-based data.

span.label: critiques → the argument that graph databases lack the sustainability foundations of XML or relational schemas
span.quote: In this sense, the critics of graph-based models do have a point; how do we validate our graphs?

span.label: extends → Vogeler on graph-based models for critical edition
span.quote: Vogeler (2021, p. 80) notes in his discussion of graph-based models for critical edition that “the formal affordance of OWL is not really exploited in Digital Scholarly Editions”.

span.label: supports → the codework literature arguing that code embodies scholarship
span.quote: The SHACL model thus provides a fascinating way to bring the intellectual contributions inherent in codework (Zundert, 2016; Antonijevic Ubois, van Zundert, and Andrews, 2018) across the “sustainability divide” that allows them to be properly valued and conserved as scholarship; at the same time, it points to a promising future model of digital work in the humanities, in which domain-specific code can live alongside the data, to be processed by more generic (and thus, hopefully, more long-lived) software platforms.

span.quote: This language solves exactly the problem that ontologies do not; specifically, in conjunction with a database that supports transactions and their rollbacks such as Neo4J, a set of SHACL constraints can ensure the consistency of data added to the graph, so that (to take the example above) a witness from one text tradition cannot be included in a stemma belonging to an entirely different tradition.

span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: The conclusion was that the ontology was not suitable for expressing the full data model employed in variant graphs, not least because all of them (Stemmarest most heavily) rely on property attributes, which RDF and OWL do not handle well and which can therefore not be suitably represented in an ontology definition.

span.label: witness —part-of→ tradition
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: For example, in the Stemmarest ontology we can say that a Witness can belong to a Tradition and also to one or more Stemmata, and that a Tradition can contain multiple Stemmata.

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED (Q-267)) · stemma —part-of→ tradition
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED (Q-267). The old span attested `stemma` only inside `Stemmarest`, the TOOL'S OWN NAME - a run of letters, not the word. This clause writes both terms and states the containment in the paper's own verb: a stemma BELONGS TO a tradition. — strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: For example, in the Stemmarest ontology we can say that a Witness can belong to a Tradition and also to one or more Stemmata, and that a Tradition can contain multiple Stemmata.

span.label: RETRACTED (DIRECTION REVERSED, AND THE TYPE IS LOOSE EITHER WAY) · SHACL —part-of→ SPARQL
span.note: RETRACTED: DIRECTION REVERSED, AND THE TYPE IS LOOSE EITHER WAY. The edge says SHACL is part of SPARQL. The span says the opposite direction of containment - SHACL has 'the ability to INCLUDE constraint components EXPRESSED IN SPARQL'. But the reverse is not clean either: SPARQL is the LANGUAGE the components are written in, not a component sitting inside SHACL, and `part-of` between two languages is not what the span asserts. Withdrawn rather than flipped into a second wrong edge. — strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Perhaps the most intriguing feature of SHACL is the ability to include “constraint components” expressed in SPARQL or Javascript, providing more or less limitless possibilities for formalising complex models.

span.label: Neo4J —operationalised-as→ variant graph
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: Constraint enforcement in Neo4J, perhaps the most popular graph database, is indeed limited strictly to data properties of nodes and relationships (Neo4J, Inc., 2022).

span.note: strength of the relation: 1

span.quote: Indeed, although ontologies have in the meantime been proposed for various aspects of digital scholarly edition (NIE-INE, 2019) and specifically for critical apparatus (Giovannetti, 2021) and an opportunity to discuss these together would be very welcome, one major motivation for undertaking the 2020 project at all was to address the concerns, frequently heard by the author in a very heavily XML-based community, that since graph databases do not tend to have schemas and certainly have no way to enforce these schemas, they lack the foundations for sustainability and interoperability that TEI XML schemas or, indeed, relational database schemas provide.

span.label: The project's conclusion was about the limits of OWL as a validation model, not about the data model.
span.quote: What the 2020 project showed, in the end, was the inadequacy of ontologies and especially OWL as a validation model for graph-based data.

span.label: The concern being answered is that graph databases lack the schema enforcement that gives XML and relational data their sustainability and interoperability.
span.quote: they lack the foundations for sustainability and interoperability that TEI XML schemas or, indeed, relational database schemas provide

span.label: an ontology can describe the model adequately and still be unable to constrain it, leaving the constraints in code
span.quote: Thus, while the Stemmarest ontology can describe the data reasonably well, it is not an adequate tool for setting constraints; these must still be described in code.

span.label: the failure traces to RDF and OWL handling properties on relationships badly
span.quote: The conclusion was that the ontology was not suitable for expressing the full data model employed in variant graphs, not least because all of them (Stemmarest most heavily) rely on property attributes, which RDF and OWL do not handle well and which can therefore not be suitably represented in an ontology definition.

span.label: RDF* supplies the missing ability to put properties on relationships, though it is early
span.quote: While it is still in an early phase of development, RDF* provides the long-awaited ability to set context for LOD statements, and promises to triple stores the same ability to set properties on relationships that graph databases such as Neo4J have always provided; this in turn has opened the way for Stemmarest, and many other projects besides, to take advantage of Neo4J’s powerful graph traversal and analysis algorithms while preserving full interoperability with LOD formats.

span.label: SHACL constraints plus a transactional store can enforce the cross-object consistency an ontology cannot
span.quote: This language solves exactly the problem that ontologies do not; specifically, in conjunction with a database that supports transactions and their rollbacks such as Neo4J, a set of SHACL constraints can ensure the consistency of data added to the graph, so that (to take the example above) a witness from one text tradition cannot be included in a stemma belonging to an entirely different tradition.
